newsitem.title: VATICAN: Castro marvels at St Peter's, tourists amazed.
newsitem.headline: Castro marvels at St Peter's, tourists amazed.

text.p: Visitors to the Vatican had to do a double take on Tuesday when the last man they expected to see -- Fidel Castro -- took a tour of St Peter's Basilica.
"Well I'll be damned!" said Emilia, an American on vacation with her husband Chester, after finding herself inside Christendom's biggest church with Cuba's communist president.
"He's an atheist. It's a wonder the church doesn't fall down," said the women from Florida, home of many exiles from Castro's Caribbean island. She declined to give her surname.

Other tourists, although kept well away, trained camcorders and snapshot cameras on the Marxist icon to show the folks back home. But at least one man whose visit was disrupted by the arrival of the heavily-guarded leader -- described by Italian television on Tuesday as a "priest-eater" -- was put out.
"I was born in Rome. I was baptised in this church. I have the same name as Saint Peter and I can't walk around because Fidel Castro's here and he's a communist," the man said.
Castro, dressed in a dark suit and flanked by bodyguards, four Roman Catholic monsignors and other officials, had a guided tour of the basilica after meeting Pope John Paul for an historic audience.
"He was bowled over," said one Vatican security official after the 25-minute tour. "He asked questions about the art."
Castro was earlier whisked across St Peter's square and into the Vatican by police cars with sirens blaring and a van with a machine-gun toting guard on the roof and another in the back.
Vatican film of the audience, at which the Pope accepted an invitation to visit Cuba next year, showed the two men shaking hands before talks in the Pontiff's private study.

The 76-year-old Pope, acknowledged as a key influence in the collapse of communism in his native Poland and the Soviet bloc, appeared frail in his white robes beside the tall, bearded revolutionary, who is six years his junior.
Inside the basilica, uniformed police with concealed guns and dozens of Castro's own security men kept tourists and other onlookers far away as the retinue snaked across the aisle.
An official Cuban television crew covered the event but no one else was allowed close enough to hear Castro's remarks.
Castro, educated as a child by Jesuit priests, gazed all around him, occasionally pointing at the basilica's marble walls or elaborately decorated ceiling and scratching his grey beard.

He admired the huge central canopy and spiral bronze columns of the main altar, designed by renaissance artist Gianlorenzo Bernini. Witnesses saw him peer below to glimpse the gold box which Christians believe holds the bones of St Peter.
Castro spent more than five minutes marvelling at Michelangelo's Pieta, a white marble statue of the Madonna holding the dead Christ.
Unlike the thousands of tourists who file past it every day, Castro was allowed behind a special bullet-proof shield erected after an attack on the masterpiece in the 1970s.
Castro then wandered over to a bronze statue of Saint Peter, a focal point for pilgrims who touch or kiss the statue's foot as a sign of faith.
Witnesses were unable to see whether Castro touched the statue because he was surrounded by officials and security men.
Castro was due later on Tuesday to return to the basilica for a visit to the tomb of St Peter.
He was also paying a private visit to the Sistine chapel, where cardinals gather beneath Michelangelo's famous ceiling frescoes depicting the story of creation to elect a Pope.
